title: LRU Cache
description: Brute force to optimized: a timestamped list scanned linearly versus a hash map combined with a doubly linked list for O(1) get and put.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with a fixed positive capacity. Implement get(key) (return the value if present, else -1, and mark it as recently used) and put(key, value) (insert or update the value; if this exceeds capacity, evict the least recently used entry first). Both operations must run in O(1) average time.

blocks.text: The cache must track not just key-value pairs, but also their RELATIVE ORDER of use, so that when it becomes full, it knows exactly which entry has gone the longest without being accessed (get or put), and evicts that one.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Small Desk With Room for Only a Few Active Files
blocks.text: Picture a desk that can only hold a few active folders at once. Every time you pull out or update a folder, you place it back on TOP of the pile. Whenever a new folder needs to be added and the desk is full, you remove the folder currently at the BOTTOM of the pile, since it is the one that has gone longest untouched.

blocks.caption: Every get or put moves a key to the "most recent" end; the "least recent" end is evicted when full

blocks.text: Before trying to track recency with timestamps scanned linearly, notice that a doubly linked list naturally maintains an ordered sequence, and moving a node to the front (or removing it from anywhere) in O(1) is possible if you already have a direct pointer to that node, which is exactly what a hash map (key to node) provides.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: get(key) needs O(1) lookup of the value, which a hash map from key to node naturally provides.

Observation 2: Every get or put on an existing key needs to mark that key as "most recently used," which means moving its node to one specific end of an ordering structure.

Observation 3: A DOUBLY linked list supports O(1) removal of a node from anywhere (given a direct pointer to it) and O(1) insertion at either end, unlike a singly linked list (which needs O(n) to find the previous node) or a plain array (which needs O(n) to shift elements).

Observation 4: Combining a hash map (key -> node) for O(1) lookup with a doubly linked list (maintaining recency order) gives O(1) for both "find and update recency" and "evict the least recent" (simply removing the list's tail, or head, whichever end represents "least recent").

This leads to combining a hash map (key to list node) for O(1) lookup with a doubly linked list maintaining usage order, moving accessed nodes to the "most recent" end and evicting from the "least recent" end, both in O(1).
Maintain a simple list of [key, value, last-used-time] entries, updating the timestamp on every access and scanning for the oldest timestamp when eviction is needed.

items: Maintain a list of entries, each with a key, value, and a "last used" counter/timestamp.
On get(key): scan for the entry with the matching key, update its timestamp, and return its value (or -1 if not found).
On put(key, value): scan for an existing entry to update, or if not found and the list is full, scan for the entry with the OLDEST timestamp and remove it before inserting the new one.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain list with timestamps directly tracks recency, correctly identifying the least recently used entry via a scan.
Both lookup (finding a key) and eviction (finding the oldest timestamp) cost O(n), too slow for up to 2*10^5 calls.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per get or put, n being the current cache size (up to capacity).
Space: O(capacity).

Limitation: both lookup and recency-tracking need to be O(1); a hash map gives O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering and eviction, together achieving the required O(1) average time for both operations.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning is unnecessary: a hash map from key directly to its corresponding node gives O(1) lookup, eliminating the need to scan for a key.

Why an array cannot achieve O(1) reordering: moving an element to the front of an array (or removing one from the middle) requires shifting other elements, an O(n) cost; a doubly linked list, however, supports O(1) removal and O(1) insertion at either end given a direct node pointer.

Combining both structures: the hash map provides O(1) access to a node given its key; the doubly linked list maintains the actual recency ORDER, with dummy head/tail sentinels simplifying edge cases at the boundaries.

The core idea: on every get or put for an existing key, unlink the corresponding node and re-insert it at the "most recently used" end; when inserting a new key over capacity, evict the node at the "least recently used" end and remove it from the hash map too.

Maintain a hash map (key to node) and a doubly linked list with dummy head/tail sentinels. On access, move the corresponding node to just after the head (most recent). On put when full, remove the node just before the tail (least recent) from both the list and the map, then insert the new node after the head.
Dry run for capacity = 2: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1), put(3,3)

blocks.caption: Hash map for O(1) lookup, doubly linked list for O(1) reordering and eviction

blocks.text: The hash map gives direct O(1) access to any key's corresponding node, eliminating the need for any scan. The doubly linked list maintains a strict recency ordering: the node just after the head is always the most recently used, and the node just before the tail is always the least recently used. Since a doubly linked list supports O(1) removal of ANY node (given a direct pointer, which the hash map supplies) and O(1) insertion at the front, both "mark as recently used" (remove + reinsert at front) and "evict the LRU entry" (remove the node before the tail) run in O(1).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for both get and put.
Space: O(capacity), for the hash map and linked list nodes.

blocks.text: LRU Cache is the quintessential "combine a hash map with a doubly linked list" design problem, a technique that shows up whenever O(1) lookup needs to be paired with O(1) reordering.

items: Forgetting to update recency on get() calls too, not just put() calls, which would break the LRU ordering.
Not using dummy head/tail sentinel nodes, leading to fragile null-checking edge cases when the list is empty or has one element.

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "hash map for O(1) lookup, doubly linked list for O(1) reordering, combined" as the design upfront, before writing any code, demonstrates the key insight clearly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "O(1) lookup AND O(1) reordering by recency", think: hash map plus doubly linked list, moving nodes to the front on access.

How would you make this thread-safe for concurrent access?
LFU Cache, a related but more complex design problem tracking frequency instead of just recency.
Any "O(1) lookup plus O(1) reordering" design problem, solvable via the hash map plus doubly linked list combination.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear-scan approach costs O(n) per operation; the hash map plus doubly linked list approach costs O(1) per operation, both using O(capacity) space.

items: Pattern: hash map (O(1) lookup) combined with a doubly linked list (O(1) reordering and eviction).
Core Idea: on access, move the corresponding node to the "most recent" end of the list; when full, evict the node at the "least recent" end.
Time: O(n) per operation for the linear-scan approach, O(1) for the hash map plus linked list approach.
Most Important Observation: a doubly linked list is what makes O(1) reordering possible, since a plain array or singly linked list cannot remove/reinsert nodes in O(1).
Interview Difficulty: a very common, must-know system-design-flavored coding interview question.
One line memory trick: hash map finds the node, doubly linked list reorders it, both in O(1).
